paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: God was working the whole time, even when it looked like nothing was happening. Naomi came home saying the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her (Ruth 1:20). Now the women tell her, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a kinsman-redeemer" (Ruth 4:14). The story that started in an empty place ends in a full one, and that should make every baker feel hopeful.

Look at who stepped up. The nearer redeemer passed on it, and Boaz bought the land and took Ruth as his wife (Ruth 4:6, 4:9-10). A redeemer is a relative who steps in so a family's name doesn't disappear (Ruth 4:10). That points to Jesus, who gave His life to rescue people (Mark 10:45), and I'm telling you, I could have used a rescue back in a junk drawer, and I got one.

Then the book ends with a family line, and there's a king at the end of it: "Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David" (Ruth 4:22). A woman from Moab, a widow gleaning in a field, ends up in David's family tree. So don't ever decide that your small, quiet, ordinary days don't matter. God can weave them into something bigger than you can see from where you're standing. The story isn't over, and neither is yours.
